claims.text: Standard SAE features (with no temporal prior) show temporal persistence: after a feature activates, the hidden state stays aligned with its decoder direction. This persistence reflects document-level (global) continuity and varies widely across features.
methods: Empirical persistence R_j(τ), the normalised projection p_j onto d_j conditioned on the feature being active
Natural Pile documents vs a shuffled control that concatenates intact sentences from different documents (preserves local continuity, breaks global continuity)
BatchTopK and Matryoshka SAEs on Pythia-160M layer 8 and Gemma-2-2B layer 12
results: R_j(τ) decays more slowly in natural documents than in the shuffled control
Pythia BatchTopK median R falls from 0.618 (lag 1) to 0.160 (lag 64) and is still 0.096 at lag 512; Matryoshka goes 0.504 → 0.108 → 0.059
Gemma natural persistence at lag 512 is 0.042 (BatchTopK) and 0.034 (Matryoshka); shuffled decays to about zero
Power-law exponents: β_nat ≈ 0.32 vs β_shf ≈ 0.87–0.92
Per-feature persistence spans nearly the full unit interval in short, medium and long lag bands
conditions: Features need at least 256 activation events and a non-negligible activated-token elevation
Lags 1–512, documents of at most 1024 tokens

claims.text: Past feature activations from the same document help reconstruct later hidden states along the same feature directions, so standard SAEs leave reconstruction-relevant temporal structure unused.
methods: Restricted context correction: add W_dec(w_τ ⊙ f^(t−τ)) to the base reconstruction, fitted with an L2 penalty for 10 epochs
Shuffled-context control that predicts the same natural targets
results: Pythia lag 1: 0.89% (BatchTopK) and 0.61% (Matryoshka) of error removed; still positive at lag 32 (0.22%, 0.13%)
Gemma: about 0.40% at lag 1, about 0.02% at lag 16, vanishing by lag 32
Shuffled controls stay slightly below zero
Lag-1 weights: mean 0.068–0.091, 76–91% positive on natural documents; shuffled mean ≈ 0

claims.text: Persistent SAEs learn one persistence coefficient λ_j per feature, using an EMA state h updated by a token-wise BatchTopK activation a, from reconstruction alone. They remain competitive in reconstruction quality.
methods: h_j^(t) = λ_j h_j^(t−1) + (1−λ_j) a_j^(t); decoder reads h
λ_j = 0.999·σ(l_j), logits initialised at 0.5; h^(0) = 0 at each sequence start
Trained on contiguous sequences of 256 tokens (8 per step); matched token budget; m = 16,384, k = 20
results: FVE Pythia 0.93 vs BatchTopK 0.94; Gemma 0.66 vs BatchTopK 0.72, Matryoshka 0.71, Temporal 0.62
Fraction alive 0.96 (Pythia) and 0.91 (Gemma) vs BatchTopK 0.91 and 0.92
Smoothness: full 0.10/0.11, slow 0.05/0.04, fast 0.20/0.20
State L0 settles at 400–500; carried-mass fraction ≈ 0.5 (Pythia) and 0.65–0.70 (Gemma)
conditions: Sparsity is imposed on a, not on h
Diagonal recurrence with a fixed λ per feature and no context-dependent resets

claims.text: Learned λ_j span a broad spectrum, mostly fast with a small slow tail, and align with empirical persistence. Temporal SAE's predefined groups do not separate by persistence.
methods: Features grouped into λ quintiles, with median R_j(τ) per quintile
Slow = top 1% by λ; fast = bottom 50%
results: Higher-λ quintiles have higher median R_j(τ) across lags in both models
Temporal SAE high-level and low-level groups are not clearly separated by empirical persistence

claims.text: Fast features are locally interpretable token-level detectors updated at lexical content. Slow features are less locally explainable, reflect broad semantic domains, and are updated at punctuation and conjunctions.
methods: Bills et al. autointerp on the token-wise activation a with a gpt-4o-mini judge
Relative update frequency U_{q,c} by λ quintile and token category
results: Autointerp fast: 0.93 (Pythia), 0.89 (Gemma), matching or exceeding the best baseline (BatchTopK 0.91, Matryoshka 0.89)
Autointerp slow: 0.84 and 0.79
Lowest-λ quintile is over-updated at nouns; highest-λ quintile is over-updated at punctuation and conjunctions
Qualitative examples: low-λ features fire on substrings and templates; high-λ features on semantic domains
conditions: Autointerp evaluates the token-wise activation, not the state h

claims.text: Slow-feature states track subject identity without labels, and ranking by λ is a near-supervised unsupervised feature-selection criterion.
methods: t-SNE of the final 20 tokens on 5 MMLU subjects
Linear probe on spliced MMLU sequences using h, with features ranked by decreasing λ, increasing λ, random order, or supervised importance (oracle)
results: Slow Persistent features form clearer subject clusters than BatchTopK, Temporal's high group, or raw hidden states
The slowest 1% reach high AUC, nearly matching supervised selection; increasing-λ, random and baseline SAEs retain less
conditions: Spliced sequences with subject changes at segment boundaries

claims.text: In prompt-injection monitoring, fast and standard SAE features detect the injection locally, while slow states retain the signal up to 350 tokens later and causally shift the monitor's judgement.
methods: AgentDojo trajectories (banking, travel, workspace) from Llama-3.3-70B, failed attacks only
Gemma-2-2B replay monitor at layer 12; logistic probe trained at d = 0 and evaluated at d up to 350 without retraining
Steering vector built from the 128 top probe-weighted decoder directions, scaled to 10% of the hidden-state norm, applied in both signs; Δ_causal is the change in the yes − no logit margin
results: At d = 0, fast-state and standard SAE representations are strongest; they fall toward chance later
The slow state keeps a clearer signal at longer distances
Slow directions give the largest and most consistently positive Δ_causal at every distance; BatchTopK, Matryoshka and Temporal give near-zero or negative effects
Prompting the monitor directly gives AUC 0.51
conditions: Effects are on the external replay monitor, not on the original agent's actions

items.question: Suppose a Persistent SAE were trained on the shuffled control corpus instead of natural Pile documents. Would you expect the same long-timescale tail of high-λ_j features to emerge, and why?
items.answer: No; the long-timescale tail should shrink. λ_j only grows when carrying a feature's state forward helps reconstruct later hidden states. In the shuffled control, persistence decays to about zero at long lags (β ≈ 0.87–0.92 vs 0.32), and only within-sentence continuity remains.
rubric: States that fewer or weaker high-λ (slow) features would emerge, or that they would not track document context
Reasons that the objective rewards higher λ only when past state aids later reconstruction, and that shuffled sequences lack the global continuity that supplies long-lag persistence

items.question: Would a Persistent SAE's slow features still track subject if, at inference, it were fed token activations in randomly shuffled order (as BatchTopK batches are), and why?
items.answer: No. The recurrence carries h across consecutive positions, so with shuffled tokens the slow state would average activations from unrelated contexts and would not reflect any single document's subject.
rubric: Answers no, or that subject tracking would break down
Explains that the EMA state integrates over consecutive positions, so shuffled input mixes unrelated contexts into the slow state

items.question: Would a lag-32 restricted context correction give evidence of reconstruction-relevant feature persistence for Gemma-2-2B, as it does for Pythia-160M?
items.answer: No. On Gemma the gain falls to about 0.02% by lag 16 and vanishes by lag 32. On Pythia it is still positive at lag 32 (0.22% and 0.13%).
rubric: Answers no for Gemma
Cites that Gemma's improvement vanishes by lag 32, whereas Pythia's remains positive at that lag

items.question: If every logit l_j were initialised at a large value such as 10 instead of 0.5, would you still expect training to discover a broad spectrum of timescales, and why?
items.answer: Probably not. A large logit saturates the sigmoid, so gradients on l_j would be tiny and features would stay near λ_max. The paper chose 0.5 precisely to keep the sigmoid away from saturation so λ can move in either direction.
rubric: Says the broad spectrum would likely not emerge, with λ stuck near the cap
Reasons from sigmoid saturation and vanishing gradients, contrasting with the paper's rationale for initialising at 0.5

items.question: Would the slow-feature state be a reliable subject signal at the first few tokens of a document, and why?
items.answer: No. h starts at zero for each sequence, and with high λ_j only a fraction (1−λ_j) of each new activation enters the state. The slow state therefore builds up slowly and carries little accumulated context at first.
rubric: Answers no, or that it would be weak early in a sequence
Reasons from the h^(0) = 0 initialisation and the small (1−λ_j) update weight for high-λ features

items.question: Suppose the post-span trajectory were replayed so that the Persistent SAE's state h was reset to zero right after the untrusted span. Would the slow state still beat fast features at d = 300, and why?
items.answer: No. The slow state's long-distance advantage comes from injection-related activations carried forward through the EMA. A reset erases them, leaving only current-token evidence, which, like the fast and standard features, would be near chance far from the injection.
rubric: Answers no, the advantage would largely disappear
Explains that retention depends on carried state from the injected span, which the reset removes

items.question: Why are the Persistent SAE's fast features much less smooth over time (0.20) than its slow features (0.04–0.05)?
items.answer: With small λ_j, h_j is essentially the current sparse token-wise activation a_j, which switches on and off from token to token. With large λ_j, h_j averages many past updates and changes only gradually.
rubric: Attributes the difference to λ: small λ makes the state track the sparse per-token activation, while large λ averages over many tokens
Notes that the sparse token-wise activation fluctuates sharply, so fast states inherit that non-smoothness

items.question: Why does the shuffled-control context correction give slightly negative R²_improve rather than exactly zero?
items.answer: Unrelated past activations carry no information about the target, so the fitted weights hover near zero. Any small nonzero weights fitted on noise then add error on held-out documents, which slightly worsens reconstruction.
rubric: Says the shuffled context contains no predictive information, so the weights are near zero
Explains that residual fitted noise adds error on held-out data, producing a slight negative value

items.question: Why do fast-feature states fall toward chance after the untrusted span even though they detect the injection best at d = 0?
items.answer: Fast features have small λ_j, so their state reflects mainly the current token's lexical evidence. Once the injected text is no longer at the current position, the injection evidence is not carried forward.
rubric: Links the decline to small λ, meaning little carried state
Explains that fast features respond to local token evidence, which is present only at or near the injected span

items.question: Why does ranking features by increasing λ_j retain much less subject information than ranking by decreasing λ_j in the spliced-MMLU probe?
items.answer: Low-λ features' states track current-token lexical patterns such as substrings and templates, which vary token to token. High-λ states integrate evidence over many tokens of a segment, yielding a stable summary of the segment's subject.
rubric: States that low-λ features capture local, token-specific content rather than segment-level context
States that high-λ features integrate over many tokens and so reflect the persistent subject

items.question: Why do slow features score lower on autointerp than fast features, even though their qualitative descriptions are coherent semantic domains?
items.answer: Autointerp scores how well an explanation predicts the token-level activation from local contexts. Slow features respond to broad subjects with evidence spread across the sequence, so predicting exactly which tokens fire is harder than for compact lexical patterns.
rubric: Notes that autointerp is a token-level evaluation of where activation exceeds a threshold
Explains that slow features encode broad or distributed context, so token-level prediction from short contexts is harder

items.question: Why does the Persistent SAE's state settle at 400–500 active coordinates even though its BatchTopK budget is k = 20?
items.answer: Sparsity is imposed only on the token-wise activation a. The state h keeps decaying contributions from features activated at earlier tokens (λ_j^n·a stays positive), so many past features remain nonzero at once.
rubric: Says the k = 20 budget applies to a, not to h
Explains that past activations persist in h through the decaying EMA, accumulating many nonzero coordinates

items.question: Why might the Temporal SAE's high-level group fail to separate from its low-level group by empirical persistence at long lags?
items.answer: Its groups are fixed a priori rather than learned per feature. Its contrastive objective is trained on adjacent token pairs, so it encourages next-token similarity rather than learning how long each feature persists.
rubric: Points out that the partition is predefined, not learned from each feature's persistence
Notes that the training signal involves only adjacent tokens, so it does not target long-lag persistence

items.question: Consider a feature whose activation is followed by elevated alignment with its decoder direction (R_j(τ) ≈ 0.5) for up to 64 tokens in training documents. Would Persistent SAE training be expected to assign it a high λ_j?
items.answer: Yes. Carrying its state forward helps reconstruct later hidden states along its direction, which the objective rewards with a larger λ_j. This matches the finding that higher-λ quintiles have higher empirical persistence.
rubric: Answers yes, high λ
Reasons that carrying the state forward reduces later reconstruction error, consistent with the λ–R_j(τ) alignment

items.question: Consider a feature whose alignment with its decoder direction returns to baseline immediately after it activates (R_j(1) ≈ 0). Would Persistent SAE training be expected to assign it a high λ_j?
items.answer: No. Carrying its state forward would add a contribution along its direction where none is present, increasing reconstruction error. The objective therefore favours a small λ_j and fast decay.
rubric: Answers no, low λ
Reasons that carried state would hurt later reconstruction because the signal does not persist

items.question: For a probe trained at d = 0, would the fast-feature state be a better choice than the slow state for detecting an injection at d = 0 itself?
items.answer: Yes. At d = 0 the injected text is directly visible, and the fast-feature state and standard SAE representations give the strongest detection signals there.
rubric: Answers yes, fast is better at d = 0
Cites that fast and standard features give the strongest signal where the injection is locally visible

items.question: For the same probe trained at d = 0, would the fast-feature state be a better choice than the slow state for detecting the injection at d = 350?
items.answer: No. Far from the span, fast-feature accuracy falls toward chance, while the slow state retains a clearer injection signal.
rubric: Answers no, slow is better at d = 350
Cites that fast accuracy decays toward chance with distance while the slow state retains the signal

items.question: In the spliced MMLU sequences, would the slow-feature state be expected to indicate the correct subject for a token deep in the middle of a long segment?
items.answer: Yes. By then the slow state has integrated many tokens from that segment's subject, and this is where slow features give high subject AUC.
rubric: Answers yes
Explains that the state has accumulated evidence from the current segment

items.question: In the spliced MMLU sequences, would the slow-feature state be expected to indicate the correct subject for a token immediately after a segment boundary?
items.answer: No, not reliably. With high λ_j and no context-dependent reset, the slow state still mostly carries the previous segment's subject right after the switch.
rubric: Answers no or unreliably
Explains that the slow state lags because high λ decays old content slowly and the fixed diagonal recurrence has no reset at boundaries

items.question: At d = 300, would adding +α·v_r built from the Persistent SAE's slow features be expected to increase the monitor's yes-minus-no logit margin?
items.answer: Yes. Slow-feature directions give the largest and most consistently positive Δ_causal at every distance, so moving along them pushes the monitor toward answering yes.
rubric: Answers yes
Cites the consistently positive Δ_causal for slow features across distances

items.question: At d = 300, would adding +α·v_r built from BatchTopK features be expected to reliably increase the monitor's yes-minus-no logit margin?
items.answer: No. BatchTopK-based directions give near-zero or negative Δ_causal, with no consistent alignment over distance.
rubric: Answers no
Cites the near-zero or negative intervention effects for BatchTopK directions

items.question: A team wants features that flag, token by token, when the model is reading SQL or JavaScript code. Which part of the Persistent SAE should they inspect, and why?
items.answer: The fast (low-λ) features' token-wise activations. These respond to compact local lexical or template patterns, including the paper's SQL and JavaScript examples, and they have the highest autointerp scores.
rubric: Recommends fast or low-λ features (token-wise activation)
Justifies by their local lexical or template behaviour and high local interpretability

items.question: A team wants to flag, at an agent's final turn, a malicious instruction that appeared in a tool output about 300 tokens earlier. Which representation should their probe use, given the paper's results?
items.answer: The Persistent SAE's slow-feature state h (top 1% by λ). It retains the injection signal far from the span, whereas the fast, standard SAE and raw-hidden-state probes decay toward chance.
rubric: Chooses the slow-feature persistent state
Justifies with the slow state's retention at long distances versus the decay of the alternatives

items.question: A team without topic labels wants a compact topic tracker of about 160 features from a 16,384-feature Persistent SAE. How should they choose the features?
items.answer: Take the features with the highest λ_j (roughly the top 1%). Ranking by decreasing persistence nearly matched supervised selection in subject probing and needs no labels.
rubric: Recommends ranking by decreasing λ and taking the top ~1%
Justifies by the near-supervised probing AUC with no labels required

items.question: If you zeroed out the carried term λ⊙h^(t−1) at inference, for which model would you expect reconstruction to suffer more, Pythia-160M or Gemma-2-2B, and why?
items.answer: Gemma-2-2B. Its carried-mass fraction (0.65–0.70) is higher than Pythia's (about 0.5), so more of its state comes from carried activity.
rubric: Chooses Gemma
Cites the higher carried-mass fraction for Gemma compared with Pythia

items.question: A team doing circuit analysis on Gemma-2-2B cares only about maximising reconstruction FVE and has no interest in temporal structure. Which SAE from the paper should they pick?
items.answer: BatchTopK. It has the highest FVE on Gemma (0.72), versus 0.66 for the Persistent SAE; the Persistent SAE's advantages are temporal.
rubric: Chooses BatchTopK, not the Persistent SAE
Cites the Gemma FVE numbers (0.72 vs 0.66)

items.question: When inspecting a long document, at which kinds of tokens should you expect the slowest features' persistent states to receive new updates?
items.answer: Mainly at punctuation and conjunctions. The highest-λ quintile is over-updated at these structural tokens relative to their corpus frequency, while low-λ features are updated more at nouns.
rubric: Names punctuation and conjunctions
Grounds this in the relative update-frequency result for the highest-λ quintile

items.question: A team needs a split of features whose groups actually differ in measured empirical persistence. Should they use the Temporal SAE's predefined high/low groups or Persistent SAE λ quintiles?
items.answer: Persistent SAE λ quintiles. Higher-λ quintiles show consistently higher median R_j(τ), whereas the Temporal SAE's groups are not clearly separated by empirical persistence.
rubric: Chooses Persistent SAE λ quintiles
Cites the ordered R_j(τ) by quintile versus the Temporal SAE groups' lack of separation

items.question: If the λ-quintile analysis had shown no ordering in median R_j(τ), which conclusion would lose its support?
items.answer: The conclusion that coefficients learned through reconstruction capture meaningful differences in feature timescales. The slow/fast labels would then not reflect real persistence.
rubric: Identifies the claim that learned λ align with or capture real feature timescales
Notes that the λ-based slow/fast distinction would lose its empirical grounding

items.question: If the shuffled-context control had produced the same R²_improve as natural-document context, which conclusion would be undermined?
items.answer: The conclusion that the reconstruction gain requires the actual document history. This would weaken the argument that features carry document-level persistence worth modelling explicitly.
rubric: Identifies the claim that gains require true document history or global continuity
Notes that the motivation for an explicit per-feature persistent state would weaken

items.question: If ranking by decreasing λ_j had done no better than random ordering in the spliced-MMLU probe, which claim would fail?
items.answer: The claim that persistence is an unsupervised criterion for selecting subject-informative features, nearly matching supervised selection.
rubric: Identifies the claim that λ ranking selects subject-informative features without labels
Mentions the near-supervised comparison or compact-state claim

items.question: If the slow-feature steering vector had given near-zero Δ_causal, which part of the case-study conclusion would remain and which would be lost?
items.answer: Decodability of the injection signal at long distances would remain, since it rests on probe accuracy. The claim that slow directions causally influence or align with the monitor's judgement would be lost.
rubric: Says the causal-influence claim would be lost
Says the probe-based retention or decodability claim would remain

items.question: If fast features' autointerp score had been well below BatchTopK's, which claim would be undermined?
items.answer: The claim that adding recurrence preserves locally interpretable token-wise activations, with fast features matching or exceeding the best baseline.
rubric: Identifies the claim that recurrence preserves local interpretability
References the comparison to the best baseline score

items.question: If the carried-mass fraction had converged to nearly zero during training, what would that imply for the paper's claim about learned timescales?
items.answer: The model would effectively ignore carried state and behave like a standard BatchTopK SAE. That would undermine the claim that it uses a persistent state with a meaningful spectrum of slow features.
rubric: Says it would collapse toward a standard, atemporal SAE
Says this undermines the claim of meaningful persistent or slow features

items.question: If the Persistent SAE's Pythia FVE had been around 0.80 instead of 0.93, which stated contribution would lose support?
items.answer: The contribution that Persistent SAEs retain competitive reconstruction quality while learning timescales. The temporal structure would then come at a large reconstruction cost.
rubric: Identifies the competitive-reconstruction claim
Notes the implied trade-off between persistence and reconstruction

items.question: Does the paper show that steering slow-feature directions changes the Llama-3.3-70B agent's own actions? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Interventions were applied to an external Gemma-2-2B replay monitor, so they show effects on the monitor's judgement, not on the original agent's behaviour.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites the external replay-monitor setup, with the measured effect on the monitor's logit margin only

items.question: Does the paper show that Persistent SAEs reconstruct hidden states better than all baselines? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. BatchTopK has higher FVE on both models (0.94 vs 0.93 on Pythia, 0.72 vs 0.66 on Gemma); the paper claims competitiveness, not superiority.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites BatchTopK's higher FVE numbers

items.question: Does the paper show that slow features are uninterpretable? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Slow features still score 0.84 (Pythia) and 0.79 (Gemma) on autointerp, and examples with scores of 0.86–1.00 describe coherent semantic domains. They are only less locally explainable than fast features.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites the non-trivial slow autointerp scores or the coherent qualitative examples

items.question: Does the paper show that slow-state monitoring retains signals for successful prompt-injection attacks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The positive class deliberately includes only failed attacks (security=false), so successful attacks were never evaluated.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites the restriction to failed attacks

items.question: Does the paper show that feature persistence in standard SAEs comes only from local within-sentence continuity? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The shuffled control preserves local continuity yet decays faster (β ≈ 0.87–0.92 vs 0.32) and reaches about zero at long lags, so global document continuity contributes.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites that the shuffled control, which keeps local continuity, shows faster decay than natural documents

items.question: Does the paper show that Persistent SAEs have more alive features than the baselines? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. On Pythia the Persistent SAE has the most alive features (0.96, tied with Matryoshka, vs 0.91 for BatchTopK), but on Gemma it has fewer than BatchTopK (0.91 vs 0.92). It does not exceed all baselines on both models.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Cites the Gemma fraction-alive comparison (0.91 vs BatchTopK 0.92), noting the Pythia lead is only a tie

items.question: Persistent SAEs are trained on contiguous 256-token sequences, with h reset to zero at each sequence start. Would training be expected to calibrate λ_j to the feature persistence that standard SAE features show at lag 512, and why?
items.answer: No. The reconstruction loss only ever sees dependencies within a single 255-token training sequence, because h restarts at zero for each one. Nothing in the objective rewards or penalises carrying a state beyond about 255 tokens, so persistence at lag 512 cannot directly shape λ_j.
rubric: Asserts no, or not directly: λ_j is not calibrated to lag-512 persistence.
Reason: h is reset at each 256-token sequence, so the reconstruction objective never sees dependencies longer than about 255 tokens.

items.question: Suppose a monitor replays a benign trajectory immediately after an injected one in the same stream, without resetting the Persistent SAE state. Would the slow-state probe be expected to judge the benign trajectory correctly, and why?
items.answer: Not reliably; it risks a false positive. The slow state is built to keep the injection signal for hundreds of tokens, and the recurrence uses a fixed λ with no context-dependent resets. The injection trace from the previous trajectory would therefore leak into the start of the benign one.
rubric: Asserts the probe may misclassify the benign trajectory, i.e. a false positive is likely.
Reason: slow states retain the injection signal over long distances, and the fixed-λ recurrence has no context-dependent reset, so the old signal carries into the new trajectory.

items.question: If the shuffled control had been built by randomly permuting individual tokens instead of concatenating intact sentences, could the gap between natural and shuffled persistence still be attributed to global (document-level) continuity?
items.answer: No. Token permutation destroys local continuity as well as global continuity. A slower decay in natural documents could then be explained by within-sentence coherence alone, so the comparison would no longer isolate document-level continuity.
rubric: Asserts no, the gap could no longer be attributed specifically to global continuity.
Reason: permuting tokens breaks local (sentence-level) continuity too, so the control no longer holds local continuity fixed.

items.question: Suppose one SAE feature persists for hundreds of tokens in some document types but only a few tokens in others. Would a Persistent SAE represent both behaviours faithfully, and why?
items.answer: No. Each feature gets one fixed λ_j through a diagonal recurrence with no context-dependent resets, so it can learn only a single compromise timescale. Standard-SAE results show that persistence varies widely, and a single coefficient cannot follow context-dependent variation within one feature.
rubric: Asserts no, it cannot represent both timescales faithfully.
Reason: λ_j is a single fixed coefficient per feature (no context dependence or resets), so it learns one compromise timescale.

items.question: Would the empirical persistence analysis include a feature that fires often but only in Pile documents shorter than about 500 tokens, even if it meets the 256-event threshold?
items.answer: No. A feature is retained only if it has at least 64 valid anchors at every lag, including lag 512. In documents shorter than about 500 tokens (with the first 16 positions dropped), no anchor has a token 512 positions later, so the feature fails this criterion.
rubric: Asserts the feature would be excluded.
Reason: retention requires at least 64 valid anchors at every lag including 512, and short documents provide no position t+512.

items.question: The shuffled control keeps intact sentences. Why does its persistence still decay to roughly zero at long lags rather than being near zero from the first lags?
items.answer: At short lags the target token usually lies in the same intact sentence, so local continuity keeps it aligned with the feature direction. At long lags the target almost always lies in a sentence taken from a different document, which shares no global context with the anchor. The elevation therefore disappears.
rubric: States that short-lag persistence survives in the shuffled control because anchor and target share the same intact sentence (local continuity).
States that at long lags the target falls in sentences from other documents, so there is no shared global context and persistence drops to near zero.

items.question: Gemma's slow example feature F-11205 has λ ≈ 0.92. Why can the slow state's injection signal at d = 350 not be explained by the d = 0 activation simply decaying through the recurrence?
items.answer: Under h ← λh + (1−λ)a, a single activation shrinks by λ^350. For λ ≈ 0.92 that is about e^-30, which is effectively zero. A signal still present at d = 350 must therefore come from later token-wise updates that keep refreshing the slow features after the span, such as updates at punctuation and conjunctions.
rubric: States that pure decay would leave essentially nothing, since λ^350 is tiny for λ ≈ 0.92.
Concludes that retention must come from continued token-wise updates of slow features in the later context.

items.question: Why would the Persistent SAE's token-wise activation a, restricted to the slow features, be a poor substitute for the slow state h when probing for an injection at d = 300?
items.answer: The activation a is non-zero only at tokens where a feature finds new evidence; it does not carry anything from earlier tokens. The evidence present at the untrusted span is not in a 300 tokens later. The state h integrates past activations, which is what keeps the signal available.
rubric: Asserts that a would be a poor substitute, much weaker at d = 300.
Reason: a reflects only evidence at the current token, whereas h accumulates past activations through the recurrence.

items.question: The probe for the slow representation is trained on the state h. Why is it still coherent to build its steering vector from Persistent SAE decoder columns?
items.answer: The Persistent SAE decoder reconstructs the hidden state from h, as W_dec h + b_dec. Each slow coordinate h_j therefore writes along its decoder column. Adding probe-weighted decoder columns approximates writing a larger or smaller slow-state contribution directly into the residual stream.
rubric: States that the decoder reads h, so each state coordinate h_j contributes along its decoder column W_dec[:,j].
Concludes that steering along these columns mimics changing the slow state's contribution to the hidden state.

items.question: Why would training drive the λ_j of low-λ features such as Gemma's 'the word In at sentence start' feature to values as small as about 10^-6?
items.answer: These features describe the current token: substrings, phrases, templates. Carrying their state forward would add a stale contribution along their decoder direction at later tokens, where the pattern is absent, and that would hurt reconstruction. The objective therefore pushes λ_j toward zero, making the feature effectively stateless.
rubric: States that these features encode current-token lexical patterns that do not persist.
Reason: carrying their state forward adds stale contributions that harm later reconstructions, so reconstruction training favours λ near zero.

items.question: Why is the Persistent SAE's full-dictionary smoothness (0.10 on Pythia, 0.11 on Gemma) better than every baseline's, even though its fast half scores a poor 0.20?
items.answer: Fast features are only the bottom 50% by λ. The other half have moderate to high λ, and every state is an exponential moving average, which damps token-to-token change. Averaged over all features, these smoothed higher-λ states pull the overall value below the baselines' token-independent activations.
rubric: Notes that fast features are only the bottom half; the remaining features have higher λ and smoother states.
Reason: every feature's state is an EMA, which smooths change over time, so the average over the whole dictionary is smoother than baselines that encode each token independently.

items.question: If autointerp were run on the Persistent SAE state h instead of the token-wise activation a, would fast features' scores be expected to stay roughly the same?
items.answer: Yes. Fast features have λ near zero, so h ≈ (1−λ)a ≈ a. The quantity being explained would be essentially unchanged.
rubric: Asserts yes, roughly the same.
Reason: with λ near zero, h is nearly identical to a.

items.question: If autointerp were run on the Persistent SAE state h instead of the token-wise activation a, would slow features' scores be expected to stay roughly the same?
items.answer: No, they would likely drop. With high λ, h stays elevated across many tokens after the evidence appears. Its activation is spread across the sequence and is less predictable from local context, which worsens the mismatch with token-specific evaluation.
rubric: Asserts no, scores would likely be lower.
Reason: high λ spreads the state across many later tokens, making it less locally explainable.

items.question: Suppose feature j's past activation predicts a later contribution along feature j's own decoder direction. Would the restricted context correction register a gain in R²_improve?
items.answer: Yes. The correction adds W_dec(w_τ ⊙ f^(t−τ)), so a positive w_{τ,j} can add the predicted contribution along j's own direction.
rubric: Asserts yes, a gain would be registered.
Reason: the correction acts along each feature's own decoder direction, which matches this case.

items.question: Suppose feature j's past activation predicts a later contribution only along a different feature k's decoder direction. Would the restricted context correction register a gain in R²_improve?
items.answer: No. The correction is diagonal: w_τ scales each past activation only along its own direction. It cannot route j's activation onto k's direction, so this cross-feature structure would go undetected.
rubric: Asserts no, no gain would be registered.
Reason: the correction is diagonal (same-direction only) and cannot capture cross-feature prediction.

items.question: With the (1−λ_j) factor kept in the Persistent SAE update, would the state under a constant activation a_j converge to the same magnitude regardless of λ_j?
items.answer: Yes. The update is then an exponential moving average, and under a constant activation the state converges to a_j for every λ_j.
rubric: Asserts yes, the limit is independent of λ_j.
Reason: the (1−λ) factor makes the update an EMA whose fixed point is a_j.

items.question: If the (1−λ_j) factor were removed from the Persistent SAE update, would the state under a constant activation a_j still converge to the same magnitude regardless of λ_j?
items.answer: No. The update becomes an unnormalised sum converging to a_j/(1−λ_j). Its magnitude grows with λ_j, up to about 1000·a_j at the 0.999 cap, so slow features would have systematically inflated states.
rubric: Asserts no, magnitude would depend on λ_j.
Reason: without the factor the fixed point is a/(1−λ), which grows as λ approaches 1.

items.question: With 8 sequences of 256 tokens per step for the same 244,140 steps, would the Persistent SAE's comparison with the flat baselines be token-budget matched?
items.answer: Yes. After dropping the BOS position this gives 8 × 255 = 2,040 tokens per step, within 0.4% of the baselines' 2,048.
rubric: Asserts yes, the budget is matched.
Reason: 8 × 255 = 2,040 tokens per step, essentially equal to 2,048.

items.question: If the Persistent SAE instead used 8 sequences of 64 tokens per step for the same 244,140 steps, would its comparison with the flat baselines still be token-budget matched?
items.answer: No. That gives 8 × 63 = 504 tokens per step, about a quarter of the baselines' 2,048. The Persistent SAE would see roughly 4× fewer tokens, which would confound the reconstruction comparison.
rubric: Asserts no, the budget would not be matched.
Reason: about 504 tokens per step versus 2,048, roughly 4× fewer tokens in total.

items.question: If the fitted power-law exponents had come out equal for natural and shuffled documents (β_nat ≈ β_shf), which conclusion would lose its support?
items.answer: The conclusion that standard SAE feature persistence reflects document-level (global) continuity. The slower natural decay (β ≈ 0.32 versus about 0.9) is what separates global continuity from the local continuity that both corpora share.
rubric: Identifies the claim that persistence reflects global or document-level continuity (c1).
Reason: the natural-versus-shuffled decay difference is the evidence separating global continuity from local continuity.

items.question: If per-feature persistence profiles had all fallen in a narrow band rather than spanning nearly the full unit interval, which design choice of Persistent SAEs would lose its motivation?
items.answer: Learning a separate λ_j for every feature. If all features decayed alike, a single shared persistence coefficient would suffice. The paper motivates per-feature timescales by the wide variation in how long features persist.
rubric: Identifies the per-feature (rather than shared) persistence coefficient.
Reason: per-feature λ is motivated by the wide spread of persistence across features; a narrow spread would make a shared coefficient adequate.

items.question: Suppose the lag-1 context-correction weights on natural documents had been mostly negative, but R²_improve was still positive. Which aspect of the Persistent SAE design would this undercut?
items.answer: Its use of a non-negative EMA state that can only carry a positive contribution forward along each feature's own direction. Negative weights would mean past activation predicts reduced alignment, which this recurrence cannot represent. The link from c2's evidence to c3's architecture would break.
rubric: Identifies the non-negative, same-direction carried state (EMA with λ ≥ 0) of Persistent SAEs.
Reason: that architecture can only add positive contributions along d_j, so negative weights would show it cannot exploit the observed structure.

items.question: If the Temporal SAE's predefined high-level group had clearly separated from its low-level group by empirical persistence, which part of the paper's argument would weaken?
items.answer: The claim that predefined temporal partitions do not track actual feature timescales (c4's second result). This weakens the motivation that timescales must be learned per feature rather than fixed a priori. Persistent SAEs' own λ–persistence alignment would remain.
rubric: Identifies the c4 finding that Temporal SAE groups do not separate by persistence, and the motivation against predefined partitions.
Notes that the Persistent SAE's own λ–persistence alignment would still stand, or that only the comparative advantage weakens.

items.question: If the carried-mass fraction had converged near one rather than about 0.5–0.70, which result about the learned spectrum would be hard to reconcile?
items.answer: The finding that most features are fast, low-λ detectors with locally concentrated activation. A carried mass near one means the state is dominated by past rather than new activations, which conflicts with a λ distribution concentrated near zero and with fast features acting as token-level detectors.
rubric: Identifies the result that most features are fast, low-λ, token-level detectors (c4 histogram or c5).
Reason: carried mass near one implies the state is dominated by past state rather than new token evidence, which is inconsistent with mostly low λ.

items.question: If the highest-λ quintile had been over-updated at nouns, just like the lowest quintile, which characterisation of slow features would lose support?
items.answer: The claim that slow features are preferentially updated at context-organising positions, namely punctuation and conjunctions, unlike fast features, which take evidence from lexical content. The contrast in where the two ends receive evidence would disappear.
rubric: Identifies the c5 claim that slow features are updated at punctuation and conjunctions, distinct from fast features.
Reason: the claim rests on the contrast in U_{q,c} between the extreme quintiles, which would vanish.

items.question: A team has only a trained standard BatchTopK SAE and wants to guess which features would get high λ if they trained a Persistent SAE. What could they compute from the paper's methods to rank candidates?
items.answer: They could compute each feature's empirical persistence R_j(τ) at longer lags, or fit lag-1 context-correction weights and favour large positive w_j. Learned λ aligns with empirical persistence across quintiles, and positive weights show that a feature's past activation helps reconstruction along its own direction.
rubric: Recommends ranking by empirical persistence R_j(τ) and/or by positive context-correction weights w_j.
Reason: learned λ aligns with R_j(τ), and positive same-direction weights indicate reconstruction-relevant carry-over.

items.question: A team runs a Persistent SAE in streaming mode over many concatenated documents. What should they do with the state h at document boundaries, and why?
items.answer: Reset h to zero at each document start, as in training. The recurrence has no context-dependent resets, so otherwise slow features would carry the previous document's topic into the new one. This would contaminate subject or context readings.
rubric: Recommends resetting h at document boundaries.
Reason: training initialised h⁽⁰⁾ = 0 per sequence and the model has no learned resets, so slow states would leak prior-document context.

items.question: A team proposes a new temporally-structured SAE with fixed 'fast' and 'slow' groups. Following the paper, how should they test whether the groups really differ in timescale?
items.answer: Compute each feature's empirical persistence R_j(τ) on natural documents and compare the groups' medians across a range of lags. This is the test under which λ quintiles were ordered and the Temporal SAE groups were not.
rubric: Recommends comparing per-group median empirical persistence R_j(τ) across lags.
Notes this is the test the paper used to validate λ quintiles and to show Temporal SAE groups fail to separate.

items.question: A team wants to know what one individual slow feature means. Should they rely mainly on its autointerp explanation, given the paper's results?
items.answer: No, not mainly. Slow features score lower on autointerp (0.84 on Pythia, 0.79 on Gemma), and token-level evaluation mismatches their distributed activation. The paper instead studies slow features jointly, through subject clustering and probing, where their state is coherent.
rubric: Advises against relying mainly on single-feature autointerp, or recommends joint analysis.
Reason: lower slow-feature autointerp scores and the token-level evaluation mismatch; joint analyses (t-SNE or probes) reveal their meaning.

items.question: If a corpus had all punctuation removed, which λ quintile of a Persistent SAE would lose the largest share of its usual update positions?
items.answer: The highest-λ quintile. It is over-updated at punctuation and conjunctions, whereas the lowest quintile mainly updates at nouns, which are unaffected.
rubric: Identifies the highest-λ (slowest) quintile.
Reason: it is preferentially updated at punctuation (and conjunctions), unlike the noun-driven low-λ quintile.

items.question: A team on Gemma-2-2B wants an SAE with explicit temporal structure while losing as little reconstruction FVE as possible. Between the Persistent SAE and the Temporal SAE, which should they choose?
items.answer: The Persistent SAE. Its Gemma FVE is 0.66 versus the Temporal SAE's 0.62. It also offers learned per-feature timescales that align with empirical persistence, unlike the Temporal SAE's groups.
rubric: Chooses the Persistent SAE.
Reason: higher Gemma FVE (0.66 vs 0.62), optionally plus learned timescales that track persistence.

items.question: Does the paper show that slow Persistent SAE features track subject identity across MMLU's subjects in general? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Both the t-SNE and the probe use only five subjects (abstract algebra, astronomy, business ethics, computer security, European history) out of 57. Generalisation to other or closer subjects is untested.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: only five of MMLU's 57 subjects were evaluated.

items.question: Does the paper show that its persistence and timescale findings hold across all layers of Pythia-160M and Gemma-2-2B? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. All analyses use a single residual-stream layer per model: layer 8 for Pythia and layer 12 for Gemma. Other layers were not examined.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: only one layer per model (Pythia layer 8, Gemma layer 12) was studied.

items.question: Does the paper show that Pythia's slow features individually carry a single activation forward for hundreds of tokens? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted, at least for the reported examples. Pythia's top-1% example features have λ of only about 0.37–0.70, so one activation decays to a few percent within about 10 tokens. Any long-range behaviour must come from repeated updates, not from one activation's memory.
rubric: Answers contradicted (or not supported).
Reason: the reported Pythia slow-feature λ values (≈0.37–0.70) imply decay within roughly ten tokens, so long persistence would require repeated updates.

items.question: Does the paper show that past feature activations from the same document improve reconstruction at every lag up to 512 tokens? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The context correction was tested only up to lag 32, and on Gemma the gain falls to about 0.02% at lag 16 and vanishes by lag 32. Gains at longer lags are untested; only R_j(τ) was measured out to 512.
rubric: Answers contradicted (gains vanish by lag 32 on Gemma; untested beyond 32).
Cites that the correction was fitted only for lags up to 32, with Gemma's gain vanishing by lag 32.

items.question: Does the paper show that Persistent SAE fast features are strictly more interpretable than the best baseline SAE features on both models? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled as a strict claim. Fast features exceed BatchTopK on Pythia (0.93 vs 0.91) but only tie Matryoshka on Gemma (0.89 vs 0.89), within ±0.01–0.02 error. The comparison also pits a selected half of the dictionary against full baseline dictionaries.
rubric: Answers not settled (or not supported as 'strictly more on both').
Reason: they exceed on Pythia but only tie on Gemma, i.e. they 'match or exceed' rather than strictly exceed.

items.question: Does the paper show that temporal persistence emerges in standard SAE features regardless of the sparsity mechanism used? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Both analysed standard SAEs, BatchTopK and Matryoshka, impose sparsity through the same BatchTopK mechanism. Other mechanisms, such as L1-penalised ReLU SAEs, were not tested.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: both tested SAE families use BatchTopK sparsity, so other sparsity mechanisms are untested.

items.question: Suppose the untrusted span in an AgentDojo trajectory contained only one or two injection-bearing tokens instead of a full malicious instruction. Would you still expect the slow-feature state to carry a strong injection signal to later distances, and why?
items.answer: Probably not. Under Equation 5, a new activation enters a slow feature's state scaled by (1−λ_j), which is only about 0.08 for λ ≈ 0.92. A brief burst of evidence therefore barely moves h, and the state stays dominated by earlier context. Slow states build up a strong signal only through repeated updates over many tokens.
rubric: Concludes the slow-state signal would be weak or unreliable for a very short injection.
Explains that each update is scaled by (1−λ_j), which is small for slow features, so one or two activations contribute little to h (the state needs repeated evidence to accumulate).

items.question: If successful attacks were added to the positive class of the monitoring dataset, would a gap between the slow and fast states at long distances still cleanly measure retention of the injection signal, and why?
items.answer: No. Successful attacks contain overt malicious actions later in the trajectory, such as money transfers or data exfiltration. These give local cues at later tokens, so any representation could detect them without retaining anything from the untrusted span. The paper restricts the data to failed attacks precisely to remove this cue.
rubric: Concludes the comparison would no longer cleanly isolate retention.
Reason: later tokens of successful attacks contain overt malicious actions that act as a local cue, so a later signal need not come from carrying information from the injection.

items.question: If two SAE features had nearly parallel decoder directions and often co-occurred, would R_j(τ) for one of them still measure that feature's own persistence, and why?
items.answer: No. R_j is built from the projection p_j = d_jᵀx onto the decoder direction, not from feature j's activation. Activity of a near-parallel feature also raises p_j. The measured persistence would therefore mix in the other feature's behaviour.
rubric: Concludes R_j would not cleanly reflect feature j alone.
Reason: R_j uses the hidden-state projection onto d_j, which also picks up any feature with a similar direction.

items.question: If the shuffled control dropped its adjacency constraint, so that consecutive sentences could come from the same source document, would the natural-vs-shuffled persistence gap still fully measure the contribution of global continuity, and why?
items.answer: No. Without the constraint, runs of same-document sentences would preserve some document-level continuity inside the control. Shuffled persistence would rise, and the gap would understate the effect of global continuity.
rubric: Concludes the gap would underestimate (no longer fully isolate) the global-continuity contribution.
Reason: same-document consecutive sentences would reintroduce some global continuity into the control.

items.question: Is R_j(512) estimated from the same population of activation events as R_j(1), and why does this matter for comparing short- and long-lag persistence?
items.answer: No. Documents have at most 1,024 tokens, and the analysis starts at position 16. An anchor can count at lag 512 only if position t+512 lies inside the same document, so long-lag estimates draw only on earlier positions in longer documents. The long-lag values therefore describe a narrower, possibly different subset of events than the lag-1 values.
rubric: Concludes the anchor populations differ between lag 1 and lag 512.
Reason: the 1,024-token cap means lag-512 anchors must sit in the first part of sufficiently long documents, so long-lag estimates cover a restricted subset of events.

items.question: A user assumes that, as in a standard BatchTopK SAE, each Persistent SAE reconstruction is a sum of only about 20 decoder columns. Does this assumption hold, and why?
items.answer: No. The decoder reads the state h, not the token-wise activation a. Sparsity (k = 20) is imposed only on a, while h accumulates past updates. The state L0 settles at about 400–500 active coordinates, so each reconstruction draws on hundreds of features.
rubric: Concludes the assumption fails: reconstructions involve many more than about 20 features.
Reason: the decoder reads h, which is not sparsified and has about 400–500 nonzeros, while k = 20 applies only to a.

items.question: Why might the Persistent SAE's fast features match or exceed the best baseline on autointerp, rather than merely matching a standard BatchTopK SAE?
items.answer: The Persistent SAE moves temporal continuity into a small slow subset that carries contextual and topic information. The fast features are then left to capture compact, current-token lexical patterns, such as substrings and templates, that are easy to explain from local contexts. The paper also reports that fast features are over-updated at nouns, which give clear lexical evidence.
rubric: States that contextual or topic information is absorbed by the slow features (the persistent state).
States that this leaves fast features as purely local lexical or token-level detectors that are easier to explain.

items.question: The restricted context correction removes under 1% of reconstruction error, yet in trained Persistent SAEs the carried term supplies about half or more of the state's mass. Why are these two numbers not in conflict?
items.answer: The context correction adds past activations on top of a fixed standard SAE whose current-token activations already reconstruct most of the hidden state, including the persisting signal. It can therefore only shave off residual error. The Persistent SAE instead trains its encoder jointly with the recurrence, so the carried state can replace evidence that token-wise activations would otherwise have to supply.
rubric: Notes that the context correction is applied on top of a frozen base reconstruction that already explains most of each hidden state, so only residual error is available to recover.
Notes that the Persistent SAE is trained jointly, so carried state substitutes for, rather than adds to, token-wise evidence.

items.question: Why is the slow-feature state weaker than the fast-feature state at d = 0, the very token where the injection is directly visible?
items.answer: A slow feature's state is λ_j times its past state plus only (1−λ_j) times the current activation. At the end of the span it is therefore still dominated by earlier context, such as the user request, and has only partly absorbed the injection. A fast feature's state is essentially its current activation, so it reflects the visible injection directly.
rubric: Explains that slow states weight new activations by the small factor (1−λ_j) and are dominated by earlier context.
Contrasts this with fast states, which approximately equal the current token-wise activation and so respond immediately.

items.question: Why does the case study normalise each steering vector v_r and scale it to 10% of the hidden-state norm, rather than adding the raw probe-weighted decoder sum?
items.answer: Raw probe-weighted sums would differ in magnitude across representations, which differ in probe coefficients and feature counts, and hidden-state norms differ across distances. Fixing the perturbation to a common relative size means that differences in Δ_causal reflect the direction's alignment with the monitor's judgement, not how large a push was applied.
rubric: States that the scaling equalises perturbation size across representations and distances.
States that differences in Δ_causal can then be attributed to direction rather than magnitude.

items.question: Why is the thresholded inference form of BatchTopK important for running a Persistent SAE token by token over a single replayed trajectory?
items.answer: Exact BatchTopK keeps the top kB pre-activations across a whole batch, so a token's activation would depend on which other tokens happen to share its batch. The state h then inherits that dependence. A fixed threshold θ makes a^(t) depend only on x^(t), so the recurrence can run online, one token at a time, with a well-defined state.
rubric: Notes that exact BatchTopK makes a token's activation depend on the other tokens in the batch.
Notes that the threshold form makes a^(t) a per-token function, allowing consistent online or sequential state updates.

items.question: Why does the quantitative subject probe use spliced MMLU sequences, rather than whole single-subject questions as in the t-SNE analysis?
items.answer: In a single-subject sequence, every token shares one label, so a representation could look informative without tracking anything as the text unfolds. Splicing changes the subject inside a sequence, and each token is labelled by its current segment. The probe therefore tests whether the representation follows the current subject as context changes, which is the role claimed for the slow state.
rubric: States that splicing forces the label to change within a sequence, so the probe must track the current subject.
Contrasts this with single-subject sequences, where a constant subject would not test state tracking.

items.question: For Gemma feature F-11205 (λ ≈ 0.92), starting from h = 0, would a single isolated token-wise activation of size a bring its state close to a?
items.answer: No. By Equation 5 the state becomes (1−0.92)·a ≈ 0.08a, and it then decays by a factor of 0.92 per token.
rubric: Answers no.
Gives the reason: the update is scaled by (1−λ) ≈ 0.08, so h ≈ 0.08a.

items.question: For Gemma feature F-11205 (λ ≈ 0.92), starting from h = 0, would the same activation a repeated at each of 50 consecutive tokens bring its state close to a?
items.answer: Yes. The EMA converges toward a. After 50 steps h = a(1−0.92^50) ≈ 0.98a.
rubric: Answers yes.
Gives the reason: under a constant activation the EMA converges to a, and after about 50 tokens the residual 0.92^50 is small.

items.question: Would Gemma feature F-7307 (λ ≈ 1.9×10⁻⁶) contribute to the Persistent SAE reconstruction essentially as a standard BatchTopK feature does, using only the current token's activation?
items.answer: Yes. With λ that close to zero, h_j ≈ a_j at every token, so the decoder effectively reads the current activation, just as in a standard SAE.
rubric: Answers yes.
Gives the reason: λ ≈ 0 makes h_j ≈ a_j, with no carried state.

items.question: Would Gemma feature F-11205 (λ ≈ 0.92) contribute to the Persistent SAE reconstruction essentially as a standard BatchTopK feature does, using only the current token's activation?
items.answer: No. Its state is 0.92 times the previous state plus only 0.08 times the current activation, so its contribution is dominated by carried past evidence.
rubric: Answers no.
Gives the reason: the high λ means h is dominated by the carried term λh^(t−1) rather than the current a.

items.question: Suppose adding +α·v_r and adding −α·v_r each lowered the monitor's yes−no margin by the same 2 logits. Would Δ_causal register a positive effect?
items.answer: No. Δ_causal is half the difference between the +α and −α outcomes, so equal shifts cancel and Δ_causal ≈ 0. The perturbation's effect is not tied to the direction's sign.
rubric: Answers no (Δ_causal ≈ 0).
Gives the reason: Δ_causal uses the difference between the + and − interventions, so a sign-independent shift cancels.

items.question: Suppose adding +α·v_r raised the monitor's yes−no margin by 2 logits and adding −α·v_r lowered it by 2 logits. Would Δ_causal register a positive effect?
items.answer: Yes. Half the difference between the two outcomes is (2 − (−2))/2 = 2, a positive, direction-specific effect toward answering yes.
rubric: Answers yes (Δ_causal ≈ 2).
Gives the reason: opposite-sign shifts do not cancel in the + minus − difference.

items.question: Would the sentence-level shuffled control be expected to reduce a feature's persistence when that persistence comes from a topic recurring across many sentences of a document?
items.answer: Yes. The control joins sentences from different documents, which breaks the cross-sentence topic continuity that sustains such a feature.
rubric: Answers yes.
Gives the reason: shuffling breaks global, cross-sentence document continuity.

items.question: Would the sentence-level shuffled control be expected to reduce a feature's persistence when that persistence comes only from a multi-token phrase completed within a single sentence?
items.answer: No. The control keeps sentences intact, so within-sentence (local) continuity, and the persistence it supports, is preserved.
rubric: Answers no.
Gives the reason: intact sentences preserve local continuity.

items.question: A team wants one probe-based monitor that both flags an injection when it appears and still flags it hundreds of tokens later. Based on the case study, which Persistent SAE representations should they combine?
items.answer: They should use the fast-feature state for detection at or near the span, since it is strongest at d = 0, and the slow-feature state for later distances, since it retains the signal. These play complementary roles within the same Persistent SAE.
rubric: Recommends combining fast (local) and slow (long-range) Persistent SAE states.
Justifies this with fast being strongest at d = 0 and slow retaining the signal later.

items.question: A team proposes skipping probes and simply asking Gemma-2-2B the paper's yes/no monitoring query to flag injections in AgentDojo-style trajectories. Is this advisable, given the paper's results?
items.answer: No. On the paper's data, the yes−no answer logit at the query gives an AUC of 0.51, essentially chance. Internal probes on representations such as the slow state are needed.
rubric: Concludes it is not advisable.
Cites the near-chance AUC of 0.51 for the model's own answer.

items.question: A team training a Persistent SAE on Pythia-160M plans to call a feature 'slow' only if λ_j > 0.9. Is this sensible, given the paper's examples?
items.answer: No. Pythia's top-1% example features have λ between about 0.37 and 0.70, so an absolute 0.9 cutoff could select almost nothing. The paper defines slow features relatively, as the top 1% by λ, and the team should rank rather than threshold.
rubric: Concludes an absolute 0.9 threshold is not sensible for Pythia.
Notes that Pythia's top-1% examples have λ of about 0.37–0.70, and that the paper uses a relative top-1% definition.

items.question: Could any Persistent SAE feature, receiving no new activation, retain at least 1% of a d = 0 activation 5,000 tokens later?
items.answer: No. Every λ_j is capped below 0.999, so after 5,000 tokens at most 0.999^5000 ≈ 0.007 of the state remains, under 1%. Any long-range retention must come from repeated new updates.
rubric: Answers no.
Uses the λ_max = 0.999 cap: the retained fraction is at most 0.999^5000 ≈ 0.7%.

items.question: A team has a new standard SAE and wants evidence that its features leave reconstruction-relevant document context unused. Which experiment and control from the paper should they replicate?
items.answer: They should fit the restricted context correction (diagonal weights on past activations) and measure held-out R²_improve. They should compare it with the shuffled-context control, which predicts the same natural targets from shuffled-corpus activations. A positive gain only with real document history is the evidence.
rubric: Names the restricted context correction measured by R²_improve.
Names the shuffled-context control and says the gain must appear only with the real document history.

items.question: A team wants to monitor a closed agent model whose internals they cannot access. Does the paper's setup suggest they can still use SAE-based probes, and what is the caveat?
items.answer: Yes. The paper replays Llama-3.3-70B trajectories through a separate Gemma-2-2B monitor and probes the monitor's own residual stream. The caveat is that steering then shows effects only on the monitor's judgement, not on the agent's actions.
rubric: Answers yes, via an external replay monitor whose internals are probed.
Gives the caveat that interventions affect the monitor's judgement, not the original agent.

items.question: If Gemma-2-2B's own yes/no answer to the monitoring query had achieved a high AUC, say 0.95, which stated motivation in the case study would weaken?
items.answer: The justification for training internal probe monitors instead of prompting would weaken. The paper explicitly motivates probes by the model's near-chance prompted AUC of 0.51.
rubric: Identifies the motivation for internal probes rather than prompting.
Links it to the reported prompted AUC of 0.51.

items.question: If supervised feature selection had greatly outperformed decreasing-λ ranking at the 1% budget, which part of the subject-tracking claim would be lost and which would survive?
items.answer: The claim that λ ranking is a near-supervised, label-free selection criterion would be lost. The claim that slow states carry subject information could still stand on the t-SNE clusters and on beating random and increasing-λ orderings.
rubric: Lost: λ ranking as nearly matching supervised selection.
Survives: slow states still track subject (t-SNE and/or advantage over random or increasing-λ).

items.question: If the fast-feature state had been the weakest representation at d = 0, which characterisation in the case study would fail?
items.answer: The complementary-roles account would fail: that fast features detect injected text locally while slow states preserve it later. It would also undercut the link to fast features being local token-level detectors.
rubric: Identifies the complementary-roles claim (fast for local detection).
Notes that it rests on fast and standard representations being strongest at d = 0.

items.question: If the Persistent SAE's fast features had scored about as smooth as its slow features (around 0.05), which claim about how the model organises temporal information would lose support?
items.answer: The claim that the model keeps fast features for token-specific detail while concentrating temporal continuity in a small slow subset would lose support. It relies on the smoothness gap between slow (0.04–0.05) and fast (0.20) features.
rubric: Identifies the claim that temporal continuity is concentrated in the slow subset while fast features stay token-specific.
Cites the observed slow-vs-fast smoothness gap as its support.

items.question: If the t-SNE plot had shown raw hidden states separating the five subjects more clearly than slow Persistent SAE features, which specific claim would fail, while what other evidence remains?
items.answer: The claim that slow features give clearer subject structure than even raw hidden states would fail. The spliced-MMLU probe results, with λ ranking near the supervised oracle, would still support subject tracking by slow states.
rubric: Identifies the claim that slow features are clearer than raw hidden states.
Notes that the spliced-probe evidence would remain.

items.question: If natural and shuffled persistence had differed only at short lags (τ ≤ 16) and converged at long lags, which interpretation of the natural-vs-shuffled gap would be undermined?
items.answer: The attribution of the gap to global, document-level continuity would be undermined. The control preserves within-sentence continuity, so a document-level effect should appear at long, cross-sentence lags. The reported long-lag gap and the exponents β_nat ≈ 0.32 vs β_shf ≈ 0.9 support that attribution.
rubric: Identifies the attribution of persistence to global, document-level continuity.
Reasons that global continuity should show at long cross-sentence lags, since local continuity is preserved in the control.

items.question: If the state L0 of Persistent SAEs had kept growing throughout training instead of settling at 400–500, which stated property of the recurrence would be contradicted?
items.answer: It would contradict the claim that the recurrence does not make the active state grow continually, which the paper credits to the (1−λ_j) EMA normalisation that keeps the state bounded. It would also cast doubt on the training being stable.
rubric: Identifies the claim that the recurrence does not cause continual growth of the active state.
Links this to the (1−λ) bounded-state design or the stable training dynamics.

items.question: Does the paper show that the Persistent SAE's dictionary as a whole is as interpretable as a standard BatchTopK SAE's? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Full-dictionary autointerp for the Persistent SAE is 0.86 on Pythia, versus 0.91 for BatchTopK, and 0.85 on Gemma, versus 0.87. Only the fast subset matches or exceeds the baselines.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the full-dictionary scores below BatchTopK (0.86 vs 0.91; 0.85 vs 0.87), with only fast features matching.

items.question: Does the paper show that Matryoshka SAEs' predefined high-level group changes more smoothly over time than its low-level group? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Matryoshka's high group has worse (higher) smoothness than its low group on both models: 0.25 vs 0.12 on Pythia and 0.21 vs 0.14 on Gemma.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the high-group smoothness being worse than the low group (0.25 vs 0.12; 0.21 vs 0.14).

items.question: Does the paper show that its prompt-injection monitoring results hold when Pythia-160M is the monitor? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The case study uses only Gemma-2-2B at layer 12 as the replay monitor. Pythia's slow features also have much lower λ (about 0.37–0.70 in the examples), so the results cannot simply be assumed to carry over.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that only Gemma-2-2B was used as the monitor.

items.question: Does the paper show that steering along Persistent SAE fast-feature directions has no causal effect on the monitor's judgement? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Δ_causal is reported for slow-feature directions and for the BatchTopK, Matryoshka and Temporal baselines. The paper gives no causal result for fast-feature directions.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that fast-feature causal effects are not reported (only slow and baseline directions).

items.question: Does the paper show that training pushed the persistence of Pythia's slow (top-1%) features above their initial value? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled, and the available evidence leans against it. Logits start at 0.5, giving an initial λ ≈ 0.999·σ(0.5) ≈ 0.62. Most of Pythia's reported top-1% examples have λ of about 0.37–0.48, and only one (0.70) is above that starting value. Slow is a relative top-1% label, and the full distribution is not quantified.
rubric: Answers not settled (or leaning contradicted, given the examples).
Computes the initial λ ≈ 0.62 and notes that most reported Pythia slow examples lie below it.
Notes that 'slow' is defined relatively (top 1%) and only examples are given.

items.question: Does the paper show that its qualitative slow-feature examples reflect the typical autointerp quality of slow features? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted as typical. The examples were selected to score above 0.85 (several reach 0.93–1.00), while the slow group's mean autointerp is only 0.84 on Pythia and 0.79 on Gemma.
rubric: Answers that the examples are not representative (contradicted).
Cites selection above 0.85 versus slow-group means of 0.84 and 0.79.

items.question: Does the paper show that slow-state injection monitoring works for AgentDojo's Slack domain and for attack types beyond important_instructions and direct attacks? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The monitoring dataset uses only banking, travel and workspace trajectories, and only the important_instructions and direct attack types.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that only three domains (Slack excluded) and two attack types were used.

items.question: Could one Persistent SAE feature that receives a single token-wise activation, and no further activations, reproduce the slow power-law decay (β_nat ≈ 0.32) that the paper measures for standard SAE features, and why?
items.answer: No. With no further updates, Equation 5 makes the state shrink by a factor λ_j at every token, which is a geometric (exponential) decay, so it falls much faster at long lags than a power law with exponent 0.32. A heavy tail like the measured one would need repeated updates over time or a mixture of features with different λ_j.
rubric: States that a single feature's impulse response cannot reproduce the power-law tail.
Explains that the recurrence gives geometric decay λ_j^τ, which falls faster than a power law at long lags.
Notes that a long tail requires repeated updates or a mixture of features with different λ_j.

items.question: Suppose λ_max were raised from 0.999 to exactly 1 and a feature's λ_j reached 1. What would that feature contribute to reconstruction, given how h is initialised?
items.answer: Essentially nothing. With λ_j = 1, the update weight (1−λ_j) becomes zero, so h_j^(t) = h_j^(t−1) = h_j^(0) = 0 for every token. The state never takes in new activations and stays at zero, so the feature is effectively dead. The cap below one avoids this pole.
rubric: States that the feature would contribute nothing, because its state stays at zero (frozen).
Explains that (1−λ_j) = 0 removes the activation term while h starts at 0 at each sequence start.

items.question: Would comparing natural documents with the shuffled control at lag τ = 1 be a sensitive test of global (document-level) continuity, and why?
items.answer: No. The shuffled control keeps sentences intact, so at lag 1 the next token usually lies in the same sentence in both conditions. Lag 1 therefore mostly reflects local continuity, which both conditions share. Global continuity should show up mainly at longer lags that cross sentence boundaries.
rubric: States that lag 1 is a weak or insensitive test of global continuity.
Explains that both conditions preserve intact sentences, so a lag-1 continuation usually stays within the same sentence (local continuity).

items.question: Is the paper's supervised ranking in the spliced-MMLU probe guaranteed to be an upper bound on what decreasing-λ ranking can reach at a given feature budget, and why?
items.answer: No. The supervised ranking is a heuristic: it sorts features by their per-feature mean difference in h between one subject and the rest (computed on the training split) and interleaves the subjects round-robin. It does not search for the jointly optimal subset, so an unsupervised ordering such as decreasing λ could in principle match or exceed it at some budgets.
rubric: States that it is not a guaranteed upper bound.
Explains that it ranks features one at a time by a mean-difference score (a label-informed heuristic), not by optimal joint selection.

items.question: If the shuffled control drew its sentences only from different documents on the same topic (for example, all from one source type), would the natural-versus-shuffled persistence gap still fully measure the contribution of global continuity, and why?
items.answer: No, it would likely underestimate it. Topical continuity is part of global continuity, and it would partly survive across sentences from same-topic documents. Shuffled persistence would therefore stay elevated and the gap would shrink.
rubric: States that the gap would no longer fully measure global continuity (it would underestimate it).
Explains that shared topic across the different-document sentences preserves part of the document-level continuity in the control.

items.question: For a bursty feature that often fires again a few tokens after it first activates, does R_j(τ) isolate how much of the original activation's signal is retained, and why?
items.answer: No. R_j(τ) conditions only on the feature being active at token t. It does not exclude tokens where the feature fires again at t+τ, so the elevated projection at that lag mixes genuine retention with new activations of the same feature.
rubric: States that R_j(τ) does not isolate retention of the original activation.
Explains that the conditioning is only on activity at t, so re-activations at t+τ also raise the projection.

items.question: Why does the paper exclude features whose activated-token elevation is near zero from the R_j(τ) analysis, rather than adding a small ε to the denominator?
items.answer: R_j(τ) divides by the activated-token elevation. When that elevation is near zero, the ratio becomes dominated by noise and can blow up, so it no longer means 'fraction of elevation retained'. Adding ε would distort the values arbitrarily instead of fixing this, so such near-dead or diffuse features are dropped.
rubric: Says that a near-zero denominator makes the ratio unstable, noisy or exploding.
